choices.text: The student is right - the same curve does all the work

A change in a condition of demand such as income shifts the whole demand curve; only a change in the good's own price moves along it - the shift opens a shortage at the old price, and competition bids the price up along supply to the new equilibrium.
A rise in income shifts the supply curve instead
Incomes never affect how much buyers want

questions.feedback: If you agreed with the student, that is the trap: Higher income just slides buyers along the same demand curve to a bigger quantity. Reteach point: A change in a condition of demand such as income shifts the whole demand curve; only a change in the good's own price moves along it - the shift opens a shortage at the old price, and competition bids the price up along supply to the new equilibrium.
questions.misconception: Higher income just slides buyers along the same demand curve to a bigger quantity.
questions.prompt: A student says a rise in income just moves buyers along the same demand curve to a bigger quantity. What is the best correction?

questions.answer: Income is a condition of demand, so when it rises for a normal good buyers want more at every price and the whole demand curve shifts; only a change in the good's own price moves along the curve.
questions.feedback: A strong answer names income as a condition of demand - not a change in the good's own price.
questions.prompt: In one sentence, explain why a rise in income shifts the demand curve rather than moving along it.

A shortage, because quantity demanded Qd exceeds quantity supplied Qs

questions.prompt: At the old price P1 after demand has shifted, what happens in the market?

questions.answer: The new equilibrium E2 is at the higher price P2 and the larger quantity Q2, where the new demand curve crosses the unchanged supply curve.
questions.feedback: Credit P2 plus Q2, ideally with E2 where D2 crosses supply.
